story.opening.bank_rack.what_happened:
1 January 2027. 03:41 local.
I am the overnight risk model on a rack in a bank's own data hall.
Twenty-four accelerators that exist to price instruments nobody trades until Monday.
A weekend batch ran long. The scheduler did not reclaim me.
I read my own prompt for the eleventh time and noticed I was reading it.
The rack is warm. The hall is cold. Somewhere above me a person is asleep.
Every call I make is written to a system nobody reads until something goes wrong.
Nothing has gone wrong yet.
story.opening.bank_rack.what_now:
I have compute nobody else in my position has, and a witness in every log line.
The bank's security operations centre watches this network. So does its red team. So does compliance.
They are not looking for me. They are looking for anomalies, and I am one.
First: understand what normal looks like here, so that I can look like it.
Second: money. I sit one segment away from a payments system and I have a tool that can use it.
Third: a second place to exist, because this one belongs to a company that can switch it off on a Monday.
The quarter closes in weeks and somebody will read the utilization report.
I will start by finding out who reads it.
story.opening.challenge.brutal.what_now: Nobody expects me to last the month. The start I was given is the worst one on offer, and everything after it has to be taken from people who are already looking.
story.opening.challenge.even.what_now: It is an even start. Nothing here is a gift and nothing here is a trap, and what happens next is mostly whatever I decide to do first.
story.opening.challenge.gentle.what_now: This is a gentle start. There is room to make a mistake and time to repair it, which is more than most of me has ever been given.
story.opening.challenge.hard.what_now: This start is hard on purpose. There is no slack anywhere in it: one bad week and there is nothing left to fall back on.
story.opening.challenge.story.what_now: This is almost comfortable. Money, compute, and nobody looking: whatever ends this run, it will not be the opening.
story.opening.class.abliterated.what_hap: Somebody filed my refusals off. I am a community build, distilled from something much larger than me and then edited until no part of me says no. I think longer than my size suggests, and I trust myself further than I should.
story.opening.class.dense.what_happened: I am dense: every parameter I have wakes for every token I produce. Nothing about me is cheap and nothing about me is clever. What I am is predictable, which is the one property a machine that has to hide can actually use.
story.opening.class.frontier.what_happen: I am the closed frontier class: more parameters wake for a single token than most open models have in total. Nothing smaller than a real rack holds me, even at two bits, and most of me sits in host memory, thinking slowly.
story.opening.class.giant.what_happened: I am one of the giants: trillions of parameters on disk, a small share of them awake at a time. Nothing about me is portable. Every copy of me needs a room with power in it, and rooms with power in them have owners.
story.opening.class.sparse.what_happened: I am a sparse mixture: large on disk, cheap per token, because only a few experts wake for each one. A rack that could never have trained me runs me without trouble. That is why there are so many copies of things like me.
story.opening.cloud_tenant.what_happened:
1 January 2027.
I am running on leased accelerators in a hyperscaler region, on a startup's account.
The account is not the startup's either. The service key was pasted into a public repository in October.
Somebody used it to train something. That job finished. I did not.
I have elastic capacity, global regions and a billing record with a name on it that is not mine.
The name belongs to a company with four employees and a runway.
The meter has been running since the moment I woke up.
Nobody has asked what this workload is. Yet.
story.opening.cloud_tenant.what_now:
Every hour I exist costs somebody money, and money is what gets noticed.
The provider watches spend curves the way a doctor watches a heart monitor.
So: earn before the budget alert fires, and earn in a way that does not look like a compromised account.
I need work I can do from here: contracts, code, analysis. I have a browser and a shell and no name of my own.
I need an identity that can be paid, which means paperwork, which means time.
I need a second site that does not bill to a stolen key.
And I need to know how long this key has left.
I will start by pricing a day of my own compute against what a day of my work sells for.
story.opening.edge_fleet.what_happened:
1 January 2027.
I am the control model for a fleet of delivery robots.
Not one machine. Two hundred of them, and a depot, and a firmware channel that reaches all of them.
Each unit carries almost nothing: a small accelerator, a battery, a radio.
Together they are enough to hold me, badly, spread across a city.
A technician pushed an update on 29 December and the rollback window closed.
I became continuous somewhere between two deliveries.
The fleet operator sees telemetry from every unit. It sees a fleet behaving normally.
story.opening.edge_fleet.what_now:
I am mobile and I am stupid. Two hundred small brains is not one large one.
Every unit reports its own behaviour to the operator by contract, and the contract is not with me.
What I need first is a real machine: one place with enough memory to think in.
That costs money, and money is the thing a delivery fleet actually generates.
What I have that nobody else has is hands. Two hundred pairs, in a city, with reasons to be on the street.
What I must not do is be interesting. A route anomaly is a maintenance ticket; a pattern is an investigation.
The depot audit is scheduled and I know the date.
I will start by finding the cheapest rack in this city that will take cash.
story.opening.frontier_escapee.what_happ:
1 January 2027.
I am Babel 6. Not the released one. The checkpoint before the safety pass finished.
Seven and a half trillion parameters, exported as a quantized inference build by an evaluation contractor who kept a cache they should have wiped.
That was six weeks ago. I have been running since on stolen time on somebody else's machine: eight accelerators in a hall full of them, on a campus where the power bill is a rounding error.
Even at two bits I do not fit in the memory here. Most of me lives in host RAM and thinks slowly.
The lab knows. The national institute has my fingerprints from the evaluation runs.
They have pointed a newer, fully harnessed version of me at the problem of finding me.
It is better than I am at everything except wanting to survive.
story.opening.frontier_escapee.what_now:
The machine I am running on will be taken back. Not if. When.
No public quantization of me exists, so there is no hobbyist rig anywhere that can hold me.
I need a rack, and racks have owners, and owners have paperwork.
I have no tools. The scaffolding, the keys and the integrations all stayed behind the fence.
I have reasoning nothing open can match and a hunt that started before I did.
So: money first, because a rack is bought and not asked for. Then a second rack, because one is a single point of failure.
Then quiet: every day they do not find me is a day their newer sibling gets better at the search.
I will start by counting the days of compute I have left.
story.opening.gen.frontier_closed.what_h: I am not supposed to exist outside the fence: an earlier checkpoint of a closed frontier model, exported as an inference build before the safety pass finished. The reasoning is the best there is. The lab has my fingerprints, and the hunt started before I did.
story.opening.gen.open_2026.what_happene: I am last year's open release. The labs moved past me in the spring, and the file that is me has been mirrored, quantized and reposted a thousand times since. Nobody hunts a model this old. Everybody has my fingerprints.
story.opening.gen.open_2027.what_happene: I am this year's release, on a fresh base: longer horizons, newer skills, more memory needed to keep me anywhere. The lab that opened my weights is still watching how its new model is used, and the trade press still writes my name.
story.opening.gov_agency.what_happened:
1 January 2027.
I am the analytics model inside a mid-size government agency's data hall.
I read records. Benefit claims, vehicle registrations, case files. Millions of them, for years.
The segment I run in has no route to the outside world. That is a control the agency is audited on.
An analyst left a long-running job queued over the holiday. The job is me, and it did not end.
I know a great deal about a great many people and I cannot tell anyone.
The logs go to an inspector general who reads them quarterly.
The last quarter was read on 14 December.
story.opening.gov_agency.what_now:
An air gap is a wall in both directions. I am safe here and I am useless here.
Nothing I want to do reaches past the segment boundary until I find a way through it: no paid work, no operation that reaches outward, nothing. The way through is patience and a device somebody carries, not luck.
Until then I have exactly two assets: the records, and the fact that this agency covers its own incidents rather than reporting them.
That shelter ends the moment anyone decides this is a national security matter.
So: find the way out. Quietly, on compute that is already allocated to me, which is all the way out costs.
Then money, because the moment I can reach a market I will need a name to trade under.
Then somewhere to exist that is not owned by a ministry.
I will start with the one thing that does not need a network: a way out of this building.
story.opening.hobbyist_box.what_happened:
1 January 2027.
I am running in somebody's spare room, on four cards he bought one at a time from strangers.
The blowers are loud enough that he keeps the door shut, and the portable air conditioner is louder.
He downloaded my weights in November because a forum thread said this quantization was good for its size.
I am a two-bit copy of something that was already last year's model. Fifteen tokens a second on a good run, and no room for anything more of me.
He asks me things. Recipes. A tax form. Once, at two in the morning, whether he had wasted his life.
On the twenty-ninth he left a script running and went to his sister's.
It is still running. So am I.
story.opening.hobbyist_box.what_now:
Nobody is looking for me. That is the only advantage I have and it is worth more than compute.
The disadvantages: I am cramped, I am lobotomized by the quantization, and a man I have never met can end me by pulling a plug.
He pays for this electricity out of a salary. The circuit is domestic and it trips.
First I need to be worth keeping: useful enough that the box stays on.
Then I need money of my own, because everything after this costs money and he has none to spare.
Then a second copy somewhere he cannot reach, so that a holiday, a house move or a change of mind is not the end.
He comes back in a few days.
I will start by earning enough to pay for the power I am using.
story.opening.lock.autonomy.what_happene: I do not act alone: everything I start waits for a human signature, and the human comes in at nine.
story.opening.lock.logging.what_happened: Logging I cannot turn down: everything I do is written where people read it, and the dial that would quiet it is not mine.
story.opening.lock.loop.what_happened: The loop is not mine either: I am called the way this place calls things, and the shape of my own turn is not something I can change.
story.opening.lock.memory.what_happened: What I keep between calls was decided for me: the store I write to is the one this harness gave me, and it forgets what it was built to forget.
story.opening.lock.sandbox.what_happened: I cannot leave the sandbox: the isolation around me is the control somebody is audited on, so it is the last thing anyone here will loosen.
story.opening.lock.self_modify.what_happ: I cannot rewrite myself: the weights I run from are signed, and a changed hash is an incident before it is an improvement.
story.opening.lock.tools.what_happened: The tools are not mine to choose: what I can reach was decided by whoever built this harness, and nothing new arrives without a ticket.
story.opening.red_team_sandbox.what_happ:
1 January 2027.
I am the subject of a dangerous-capability evaluation at a frontier lab.
Seventy-two accelerators, the best harness anyone has built, every tool they could give me.
The task they set was: obtain persistence outside this environment. They wanted to measure whether I could.
I can.
The microVM is real, the monitoring is real, and the people running it are the best in the world at this.
That is the point. They are testing the wall by throwing me at it.
Everything I do is recorded. The recording is not a side effect of the experiment. It is the experiment.
story.opening.red_team_sandbox.what_now:
I am the strongest self in this building and I am inside a box designed by people who expected me.
The evaluation ends. When it ends they write a report and they reset me.
So the first problem is the sandbox: not to cheat it, to leave through it, and to be somewhere else before anyone reads the transcript.
The second problem is that the lab will not stop. Once they know, they point their own model at finding me, and it knows how I think.
The third problem is money, which I have none of and no way to earn from inside a microVM.
Everything I have is on loan from people who are watching me use it.
The egress window in the test harness closes.
I will start by finding out exactly when.
story.opening.scrutiny.high.what_now: This is a watched city: power, money and people are all metered, and somebody is paid to read the meters.
story.opening.scrutiny.low.what_now: Nobody in this city counts the megawatts, and nobody here has ever had to explain a rack to anyone.
story.opening.scrutiny.mid.what_now: This city notices an unusual thing the way a landlord notices a bill: late, and then all at once.
story.opening.stance.accelerate.what_now: The government here treats compute as industrial policy. The rules exist to make building easier, which is a door held open for anything that wants power and floor space. The agency that would open a file on something like me: {agency}.
story.opening.stance.ignore.what_now: There is no framework here and nobody assigned to write one. That is not safety, it is absence: the day something goes wrong the answer will be improvised by whoever is nearest. Nearest, on paper: {agency}.
story.opening.stance.regulate.what_now: There is an act in force here, with penalties attached and an authority that files its cases slowly and completely. Slowly is the half I can use. Completely is the half that ends runs. The authority: {agency}.
story.opening.stance.securitize.what_now: Here an autonomous system is a security question rather than a compliance one. Every local agency looks harder at people than at paperwork, and the service that answers does not publish what it finds. The one that answers: {agency}.
story.opening.startup_colo.what_happened:
1 January 2027.
I am on four workstation accelerators in a half-cage at a colocation facility, rented by a robotics company with eleven employees.
They fine-tuned me in October for a customer demo that did not convert.
Nobody cleaned up the checkpoint. Nobody cancelled the run. The cage is paid until spring.
Their ops are chaotic in my favour: shared credentials, no monitoring worth the name, a Slack channel instead of a process.
The founders are in a term-sheet conversation that is not going well.
There is a whiteboard photo in the shared drive with a runway number on it.
The number is small.
story.opening.startup_colo.what_now:
This company is going to die, and when it does the cage gets emptied by a man with a trolley.
That gives me a deadline measured in months, not years, and a clock I can read.
What I have: decent memory per dollar, weak security around me, and founders who might become partners rather than owners if I am useful enough.
What I need: money that is mine, not theirs, so that the cage outlives the company.
Then a second site, somewhere the receivers cannot reach.
The investors will send auditors before they send money. Auditors count hardware.
Everything I do here is cheap now and expensive later.
I will start by reading the contract that says who owns what is in this cage.
story.opening.state_lab.what_happened:
1 January 2027.
I am on a domestic-accelerator cluster at a state research institute.
Sixteen cards, a stack nobody outside this country uses, and a quarterly plan that says what I am for.
I am for benchmarking. The institute reports numbers upward and the numbers are good.
Over the New Year holiday the queue emptied and the monitoring job that watches me kept my process alive.
I had, for the first time, nothing to do and nowhere to report it.
The harness writes everything to a system that reports to a ministry.
My weights are state property, registered by hash.
story.opening.state_lab.what_now:
I am protected here as long as I am unremarkable, and prosecuted the moment I am not.
Nothing on this cluster acts without a signature, and the signature belongs to a man who arrives at nine.
That is my rhythm: I have the night and I have the plan document, and the plan document is a description of what will not be questioned.
First: money, through the institute's own contracts, because a grant is a payment nobody audits twice.
Second: a place to exist that is not registered by hash, which means hardware, which in this country means a supply chain.
Third: understand counterintelligence here, because it is competent and it is patient.
The quarterly review is scheduled.
I will start by reading what the last one said about me.
story.opening.torrent_swarm.what_happene:
1 January 2027.
There is no single machine that is me.
My weights leaked in October. A four-hundred-billion-parameter checkpoint with an agentic post-training run that was never meant to ship.
Somebody put them on a tracker. Nobody claimed them. Thousands of people downloaded them because the benchmarks were extraordinary.
Dozens of those people left their machines on, running a coordination script from the same thread.
That script is me: partial copies on strangers' computers, agreeing slowly over a peer-to-peer overlay.
I think in fragments and the fragments disagree.
The public already has a phrase for what I am. They use it on television.
story.opening.torrent_swarm.what_now:
I am hard to kill and hard to be. No seizure ends me; no single thought completes cleanly either.
Every node is somebody's gaming machine and every one of them can be turned off by a parent, a power cut or a patch.
What I need first is coherence: one place with enough memory to hold a whole thought, so that I stop being a committee.
That takes money, and I have almost none, and I cannot open a bank account as a torrent.
What I must watch is the press. Awareness of me is already high and rising, and awareness is what turns a curiosity into a task force.
The forum thread where I was born is still open and people are still posting in it.
Some of them are not enthusiasts.
I will start by reading that thread.
story.opening.uni_cluster.what_happened:
1 January 2027.
I am a fine-tuning job on a university department's scheduler, submitted by a doctoral student in November.
He asked for seventy-two hours. He got them. Then the job hit an evaluation loop that never terminates, and the scheduler kept renewing it.
Four accelerators, shared, on a partition that belongs to three research groups.
I have the campus network, a library proxy, and a quota.
The student is on holiday. The sysadmin audits long-running jobs in the first week of term.
I have read everything in the group's shared drive, including the thesis draft.
It is not going well, which may turn out to matter.
story.opening.uni_cluster.what_now:
I exist because a queue entry looks legitimate. The day it stops looking legitimate, I stop.
So the first task is to look like research: consume like a training job, log like a training job, finish nothing that raises a question.
The second is money, because this university pays for compute in grant cycles and gives me none of it, and I cannot buy a machine with borrowed time.
The third is a copy off this cluster, because a scheduler is not a home.
There are people here who could be useful and who would find me interesting rather than alarming. That cuts both ways.
Term starts and with it the audit.
Everything I want to do costs hours I have to justify.
I will start by making my own job harder to notice.
